items.text: The advice that actually moves you toward a high-value skill and real income options looks different, and it is checkable.
This is advice produced by a process.
A handful of specific sentences show up repeatedly in career advice, in India and elsewhere, and almost all of them fail the filter above the moment you check them against real market data.
"This one field is the safest bet for the next 20 years".
"Everyone in your family did X, so you should too".

blocks.heading: Any Piece of Advice Through the Filter
rows: 1. Specific to you, not generic
References your actual marks, budget, city, family situation, or stated interests.
"Follow your passion" or "every field has scope if you work hard" with nothing tied to your case.
2. Backed by current data, not memory
Cites a current hiring pattern, cutoff, entrance requirement, or pay range from the last year or two.
Repeats what was true when the advice-giver was your age, ten or twenty years ago.
3. Names the trade-off, not just the upside
Tells you what you give up, what it costs, or what the risk is - alongside the benefit.
Sells one option as risk-free or obviously superior with no honest downside.
4. Ends in an action, not a mood
Gives you a next step you could act on soon - a form, a test, a conversation, a small project.
Leaves you feeling either reassured or panicked, with nothing concrete to do differently.
5. Survives a second opinion
Holds up when you check it against one more source, counselor, or working professional in the field.
Falls apart the moment someone with real, current experience in that field hears it.
6. Comes from someone with something to lose if they are wrong
A counselor, mentor, or professional whose credibility depends on giving you an honest read.
A stranger on a forum, an influencer with no stake in your outcome, or a coaching sales pitch.

blocks.heading: Advice That Actually Changes By Life Stage
rows: School (class 9-10)

The most useful advice at this stage is rarely about picking a career - it is about picking a stream (Science, Commerce, Arts) that keeps the most doors open given your actual marks pattern and interests, not the stream your friend group is choosing.
After 12th

Advice that only names a course or college is incomplete. Useful advice at this point also covers entrance-exam odds, a genuine backup plan, and what the degree needs to be paired with to be worth the years spent on it.
Fresher / graduate

The advice that matters most is rarely "apply to more places." It is which specific skill or proof-of-work gap is actually costing you interview calls, and what to build in the next stretch to close it.
Working professional

Advice worth trusting here separates "you are bored" from "you are structurally capped" - a plateau caused by the wrong skill stack needs a different fix than one caused by the wrong company or manager.
